newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan chart course for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan chart course for peace talks.

text.p: India and Pakistan, anxious to end the conflict that has dogged them since independence 50 years ago, on Monday set an agenda for peace talks which analysts saw as a step forward rather than a breakthrough.
Peace and security -- along with the hitherto intractable Kashmir dispute -- featured at the top of the agenda, announced after weekend talks between foreign ministry officials.

The two sides agreed to set up working groups to tackle a range of issues, including trade and economic cooperation and a military confrontation on the Siachen Glacier. They also promised to halt "hostile propaganda and provocative actions".
Pakistan had voiced concern before the talks at the reported movement of Indian missiles near its border, the death of an army major in border gunfire and an alleged air space violation.
India has denied deploying its new Prithvi medium-range missiles and said the air space violation never took place.
"The fact that the talks took place despite the events proves that the basic practical approach remains," India's former foreign secretary, J.N. Dixit, told Reuters in New Delhi.
"It is good the talks have not broken down and they have agreed on a mechanism and to continue to talk, but I don't think there was any breakthrough on substantive matters," he said.
Dixit led the Indian team in earlier talks which collapsed in January 1994 amid acrimony over Kashmir, of which India controls two thirds and Pakistan the rest.

Ghani Jafar, an analyst at Islamabad's Institute of Regional Studies, said Pakistan could take comfort from India's acceptance of Jammu and Kashmir as an outstanding issue. India has in the past described the Kashmir question as closed.
He said Pakistan had apparently resisted Indian attempts to link the Siachen stand-off with Kashmir, but noted that the two sides had failed to set up working groups.
"It was generally being said that working groups would be formed, but that has not happened," he said.
The joint statement said only that the two sides had agreed "to set up a mechanism, including working groups at appropriate levels", to address the agreed eight-point agenda.

It said the foreign ministry secretaries, due to meet next in New Delhi in September, would themselves handle the top two agenda items -- peace and security, including confidence-building measures, and Jammu and Kashmir.
A Western diplomat, who asked not to be named, said several questions remained on the procedural nitty-gritty.
"When will the working groups start? Will they meet simultaneously? And will they be inter-dependent?" he asked.
Pakistan has in the past stressed that lack of progress on what it sees as the core issue of Kashmir would make it difficult, if not impossible, to move forward elsewhere.

Prime Ministers Nawaz Sharif of Pakistan and Inder Kumar Gujral of India, who met at a regional conference in the Maldives in May, have put their personal weight behind the latest effort to reduce tension between South Asia's threshold nuclear powers.
But both men are under pressure from hardliners opposed to any compromise on Kashmir and, while Sharif can count on a huge parliamentary majority, Gujral heads a fragile coalition.
Asked if the momentum of talks could be sustained, Dixit said: "It depends on what government is in power here -- and there -- in six months or eight months or a year."
Both prime ministers have spoken of the need to divert money spent on costly military programmes into social and economic development to bring prosperity to their countless poor.
Pakistan is keen to lighten the burden of defence spending -- which, with debt servicing, drains most of its budget -- but says it must respond to perceived threats from its giant neighbour.
India and Pakistan have gone to war three times in the past half-century, twice over Kashmir.

New Delhi demands that Islamabad halt what it calls a proxy war in the Himalayan region. Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms, trains and funds Kashmiri militants fighting Indian rule, saying it gives only moral and diplomatic support.

Islamabad wants mainly Moslem Kashmiris to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India. India says Kashmir is an integral part of its territory and also claims the Pakistani-held sector.
